items.title: What’s new in AI infrastructure and orchestration in October
items.summary:
The Google Cloud AI Infrastructure team had another busy month in October, filled with new product launches and updates to power today’s AI and agentic workloads scalably and efficiently. We were also honored to share our progress with customers, partners, and the broader community at leading industry events, including NVIDIA GTC, PyTorch Conference, and AGNTCon + MCPCon. Let’s dive in!

Product, technology, and tools updates

  • New compute service: Agent Compute Engine is a purpose-built compute service providing high-performance, hardware-isolated microVM sandboxes alongside expanded agent governance capabilities like Agent Gateway and Agent Registry, all in the service of securing and scaling autonomous AI agents. Its primary benefits include rapid sub-second activation, extreme workload density through copy-on-write memory sharing, enterprise-grade security and identity management, and cross-cloud observability.

  • AI Hypercomputer updates: At NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 we announced updates to our agentic infrastructure, including to A5X instances powered by the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, Virgo Network scale-out fabric, and Managed Lustre storage. These co-engineered advancements provide enterprises with accelerated performance, enhanced sovereign AI controls, while advanced Confidential Computing capabilities help you train and deploy complex multi-step models securely and efficiently.

  • GKE product update: CPU startup boost for GKE, in preview, uses Kubernetes In-place Pod Resize to dynamically elevate container CPU resources during initialization and scale them back down to steady-state levels without having to restart the containers. This feature removes startup throttling and accelerates cold starts by up to 2x for demanding workloads, helping to lower cloud infrastructure costs.

  • GKE product update: The preview of the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) brings low-touch deployment, automated lifecycle management, enterprise credential security, and fleet-wide governance to Wiz's eBPF runtime threat detection for both Standard and Autopilot GKE clusters.

  • Modernization tools: Together at last. Google Cloud Modernize brings Google Cloud’s migration and modernization tools, including Migration Center, Google Cloud VMware Engine, Google Cloud Mainframe Modernization and our new EKS-to-GKE Migration Agent, into a single portfolio. Enterprise teams now have purpose-built agentic capabilities across infrastructure assessment, platform modernization, and application modernization.

  • Cloud Run product update: Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run automatically scale worker pools based on Temporal task queue demands and scale down to zero when idle. This integration eliminates cluster management, lowers costs, using Temporal Worker Versioning to safely handle stateful, long-running workflows and AI agent workloads.

  • New open-source product: llm-d 1.0 is an open-source, Kubernetes-native serving stack that turns a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool, unifying distributed LLM inference across mixed Google Cloud TPU and GPU fleets. Co-founded by Google and partners, it provides production-ready benefits such as cache-aware routing, tiered KV cache offloading, and priority-based flow control to dramatically improve context reuse, reduce time-to-first-token latency, and efficiently scale multi-tenant agent workloads.

  • New open-source product: Working with Meta, we open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch stack that integrates Google TPUs directly into the PyTorch ecosystem alongside GPUs and CPUs. Now developers can train, serve, and deploy models natively on TPUs using familiar frameworks like Hugging Face, vLLM, and TorchTitan.

  • Google Distributed Cloud updates: Organizations that operate under strict sovereignty mandates would love to use AI to help them process data, but can’t send it to the cloud. The latest version of Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped brings frontier AI models and multimodal enterprise search with Gemini into these isolated environments. In addition, GDC air-gapped supports NVIDIA HGX B300 systems based on the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra architecture, and features enhanced networking and security capabilities. 

  • Edge inference product: Google open-sourced ML Drift, a cross-platform on-device GPU compute engine built for LiteRT that abstracts hardware complexities across OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU. The framework delivers peak performance, enhanced 5D tensor support, and memory efficiency for both classical machine learning workloads and advanced generative AI models at the edge.

  • Open-weight model support: Reflection's Beam is an open-weight, 501-parameter model released under an Apache 2.0 license designed specifically for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. We announced day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for service Beam on AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure.

Practitioner guides and how-tos

  • AI network reference architectures: In Networking for AI inference model serving - GKE only and for all other backends, learn about reference architectures for AI inference model serving that provide centralized governance and private IP routing using Private Service Connect, Apigee API Management, and Model Armor. These architectures simplify multi-model scaling and prompt security across GKE, Cloud Run, and hybrid clouds. 

  • How-to guide: A Tale of TPU Observability on GKE: Part 2 - Dynamic Slicing Enhancements breaks down GKE's new Dynamic Slicing observability tools and metrics for next-generation v7 TPUs through an engaging, story-driven observability guide featuring Alex, a lead AI platform engineer. Explore the step-by-step diagnostic workflows with real-world examples and handy command-line snippets. Check out Part 1 here.

Customer and partner updates

  • AI21 achieves an 83% reduction in time-to-start for AI workloads with AI Hypercomputer: Frontier lab AI21 needed a new stack on which to train its Jamba family, and chose AI Hypercomputer configured with GKE on A3 and A3 Ultra instances. By doing so, AI21 says it cut high-priority job wait times from 72 hours to 12, and manual scheduling interventions from 20 per week to zero.

  • Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs: Visko, an AI startup developing interactive world models, deployed an end-to-end live inference pipeline that combines video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio onto a single Cloud TPU slice. In this blog, the team discusses how it engineered the pipeline, the architectural optimizations it made, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI.

  • ZenteiQ scales physical AI inference 4x with GKE and llm-d: In order to pre-train models that understand physical laws, governing equations, and numerical solvers, Indian AI startup ZenteiQ designed and built a large-scale batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that runs across multiple model families and feeds verified datasets into training runs. GKE and GKE Inference Gateway gave ZenteiQ the inference-routing layer within its pipeline to scale aggregate inference throughput 4.07x and grow daily output from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion generated tokens for every 1,000 accelerators.

  • Palo Alto Networks modernizes cloud-delivered security service: Palo Alto has worked with Google Cloud since 2018 to deliver its Prisma Access security service, and it was time to update it. In order not to compromise its security guarantees, Palo Alto separated the platform into two independently scalable layers: an ingress layer that handles traffic routing and forwarding running on GKE, with Axion C4A instances; and a security layer that handles threat inspection, running on dedicated single-tenant VMs fronted by an Internal Load Balancer. Each layer can now scale, update, and operate independently. 

  • Oracle is the first hyperscaler to provide TPUs outside Google Cloud: By deploying Google TPUs, Oracle is broadening the range of AI chips available through its Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), and giving customers more options for running AI workloads. Google TPUs on OCI will be available in 2027.

Research, reports and deep-dives

  • New resource: As enterprise organizations shift from isolated AI experiments to production-scale systems, different departments — from engineering and finance to executive leadership — often speak different technical dialects; The Encyclopedia of AI Infrastructure bridges that communication gap by demystifying complex infrastructure jargon.

  • Analyst report: We are thrilled to announce that Google was named a Leader in the inaugural 2026 IDC MarketScape for Agentic AI Platforms. 

  • Deep dive: A companion technical guide describing the architecture of Agent Compute Engine and how Google’s Gemini team needed both the isolation of a VM and the speed and density of a container to deliver personal agents for every Gemini user.

September 2026

Product, technology, and tools updates

Google Kubernetes Engine updates: The GKE team is all about improving the scalability of the platform, and in September, those improvements came in many shapes and sizes:

  • New feature: Need an execution runtime with higher density for your agentic workloads? We engineered the new open-source GKE Agent Substrate to run millions of sandboxes with 10x higher density than standard container runtimes. Agent Substrate also delivers sub-500ms resume operations at over 500 suspend/resume activations per second with a native zero-trust kernel and network isolation. 

  • Product update: GKE now has scale-to-zero capabilities built-in. No need to configure complex components to scale your workloads down, thanks to the HPA with the Autoscaling Metric and support for KEP-2021, which do the job for you, out of the box. Read the blog to learn more. 

  • Product update: Further, the GKE HPA (with the above-mentioned Autoscaling Metric) now lets you scale up and down based on custom PromQL metrics, in addition to standard metrics, allowing you to trigger workloads according to conditions that are meaningful and unique to your business. Read more here. 

  • New feature: Yet another scalability feature is GKE Pod snapshots, which lets you save the running state of your workload, including CPU and GPU memory, and restore it on demand. According to internal tests, GKE Pod snapshots can reduce AI inference start-up by as much as 89%. Learn more here.

  • New migration tool: Finally, if you’ve always wanted to migrate your container workloads from AWS EKS to GKE but feared a daunting, high-friction engineering endeavor, we’ve just launched GKE agentic migration, a purpose-built agent plugin that replaces brittle, ad-hoc prompting with an AI-assisted migration pipeline protected by deterministic guardrails. Designed as a compilation of agent skills and a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, it uses AI to translate complex AWS EKS IaC and Kubernetes manifests directly into GKE landing zones. Get started with the onboarding guide.

  • Feature updates: Reinforcement learning (RL) and evaluation workloads are a beast: In a standard agentic RL loop, an LLM policy generates actions like code snippets on GPUs and executes them inside isolated CPU sandboxes to observe a reward signal. However, when scaling up this loop to support tens of thousands of parallel rollouts, infrastructure bottlenecks emerge, for instance idle accelerators, image cardinality, and a saturated control plane. To help, we developed GKE Agent Sandbox optimized for RL, plus an Agent Sandbox RL orchestration SDK and native integrations for popular RL gyms and harnesses. All are now generally available, and you can learn more here.

Storage updates: AI trains and creates lots of data, and that data has to live somewhere — in block storage systems, file systems, object stores and databases. We announced enhancements to our storage portfolio to help this critical layer roll with the agentic punches:  

  • Product update: Filestore agent volumes offer high-performance, elastic, persistent file storage for agentic workloads. Thanks to its tight integration with GKE Agent Substrate and GKE Agent Sandbox, Filestore agent volumes automatically allocates and attaches a dedicated, isolated file workspace to GKE agent sandboxes in milliseconds. Request access to the preview here. 

  • New product: If you run generative AI and RAG data layers  — think Milvus, Pinecone, Qdrant, Vespa, Redis, and in-memory context caching — you may want to take a look at the M4N family of VMs, now GA, which offers the highest per-core IOPS and throughput of leading hyperscalers. Paired with Google Cloud's custom Titanium offload architecture and paired with Hyperdisk Extreme, M4N instances deliver up to 25,000 MiB/s (25 GiB/s) of aggregate host storage performance and up to 1 million IOPS. 

  • New product: Another new Compute Engine product, Z4D, is GA, and a strong storage solution for AI/ML training and inference workloads. When configured as a bare metal instance, Z4D provides both the high local SSD (LSSD) capacity and low latency required by agentic microVMs, so you can run thousands of isolated sandboxes per host with native performance and efficiency. Learn about Z4D machines here.

  • Product update: Today’s AI training and inference pipelines create data faster than most storage management systems can keep up, creating challenges for teams trying to understand their storage estates. A new version of Storage Intelligence advisor makes it easier to answer the question: "What’s in my buckets?" and quickly identify unexpected changes. Then, enhanced batch operations let you automate bulk changes across your buckets — say, move storage classes, mass-delete stale or temporary data, or apply metadata, tagging, retention, or encryption changes. Learn about the latest in Storage Intelligence advisor here.

  • New product: Last but not least, a new version of AlloyDB for PostgreSQL brings together pioneering Google infrastructure — Colossus distributed file system, and Jupiter network — to power a new, no-compromises database architecture for the agentic era. 

Practitioner guides and how-tos

  • How-to: Wish you could make GPUs and TPUs scattered around the globe behave as a single pool behind a single entry point? In this blog, we show you how to do just that. At the edge, the multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway focuses on global, multi-region traffic distribution and high availability. Beneath that, the LLM-d router handles complex, memory-aware scheduling algorithms to keep utilization high. This architecture is deliberately runtime-, model-, and accelerator-agnostic, and in tests, routing traffic through the multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway added less than 1% overhead.

  • Guide: Using or planning to use GKE on TPUs for AI model training or inference? Training massive Large Language Models (LLMs) or running high-throughput inference serving represents a significant investment in specialized AI hardware, such as Cloud TPUs and GPUs. To get the most out of every dollar spent, you need to understand workload lifecycle metrics in GKE. This detailed guide explains how to turn opaque cluster behaviors into actionable telemetry.

Customer and partner updates

  • GKE customer: Learn why gaming startup SeaVerse relies on GKE Agent Sandbox for its multi-tenant workloads, and how the platform helped it decrease its infrastructure costs by 60%. 

Research, reports and deep-dives

In case you missed it, we’re also thrilled to share that Google has been named a leader, including achieving the highest score on either product or strategy, in three key analyst reports from Gartner and Forrester. 

  • Google is a leader in The Forrester Wave™: Public Cloud Platforms, Q3 2026: Highest overall score of any cloud provider!
  • Google named a Leader in 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Strategic Cloud Platform Services: Positioned furthest for “Completeness of Vision” of all vendors evaluated.
  • Google is a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Container Management: Positioned highest in “Ability to Execute” of all vendors evaluated.
  • Google Cloud achieved a Gold rating in the latest SemiAnalysis ClusterMax 3.0 report, which evaluates the reliability, performance, support, pricing, and security of GPU providers globally. See the full report for more.

August 2026

Product, technology, and tools updates

  • Product update: Filestore, Google Cloud’s first-party, secure, scalable NFS file service, has emerged as a popular storage platform for AI and agentic workflows, and now, it’s even better suited to the task, with a new backend storage layer built directly on Colossus, Google’s foundational distributed storage system. This new backend lets you provision IOPS independently from storage capacity, and is deeply integrated with GKE. In AI environments, this can help you service so-called agentic swarms — large groups of agents that need to read and write to a common dataset — without a drop off in performance. For more, check out the blog post. 

  • New feature: gVisor sandboxes are now available in distributed Ray clusters on GKE. In partnership with Anyscale, we introduced an experimental library for Ray that brings gVisor, Google’s open-source application kernel, directly into distributed Ray clusters. gVisor provides lightweight environments with stronger isolation than ordinary containers, plus fast startup times and low memory overhead. To try out these sandboxing capabilities on GKE, head over to the Ray sandboxing User Guide.

  • Product update: Looking for high-performance, easy-to-use infrastructure on which to run a personal AI agent, but don’t want to spend a lot of money? New Cloud Run instances are dedicated, singleton compute runtimes on Cloud Run that won’t shut down when the agent is idle. Better yet, the cost to run a Cloud Run instance with 1 vCPU and 1 GiB of memory continuously for 30 days is just $5.70.  

Practitioner guides, documentation and how-tos

  • How-to guide: Big news in Model Context Protocol (MCP) land: As of the 2026-07-28 specification, the protocol core is “completely stateless. The handshake is gone. The initialize / initialized handshake (SEP-2575) and the logical Mcp-Session-Id header (SEP-2567) have been removed entirely. Instead, every request is now self-describing and independent.” Whoa. Learn more about the changes that the latest MCP specification brings, and more importantly, how to implement them, in this Google Developers blog.  
  • Guide: Real-time AI systems make a mess of traditional network load balancing techniques. “Instead of handling isolated requests, the backend has to manage a continuous, live bidirectional stream. You’re dealing with a constant stream of audio chunks, transcripts, model outputs, and synthesized speech flowing back and forth simultaneously.” Things only get worse when the user gets involved. “The server has to immediately halt its current speech generation, pivot to update the context, maybe trigger a new tool, and start drafting a different response; this must be done without dropping the connection.” For a new approach to managing load in the AI era, read Scaling real-time AI agents with session-aware load balancing.
  • How-to: Learn how to build an elastic, scalable LLM inference platform on GKE, even with a mix of different GPU accelerators. The proposed architecture combines Capacity Advisor and Compute Advisor, plus high-performance storage like RunAI:model streamer or GCPFuse with parallel downloads. Get all the details here.
  • Documentation: The thing about hosts with GPUs or TPUs is that you can’t use live migration to update them, setting up a maintenance challenge. In this new docs page, learn how to update accelerator-equipped hosts according to your tolerance for downtime for your training and inference workloads.    
  • Documentation: Advanced Compute Images, or ACIs, are standardized image stacks for AI/ML and HPC infrastructure, so you don’t need to manually build your own custom images. In this new docs page, learn how to create an ACI image using the Google Cloud CLI, console, or SchedMD's Slurm workload manager. 
  • Guide: AI workloads are notoriously difficult to architect, resource-intensive, and bursty, which can also lead to scaling bottlenecks and large pools of underutilized — or misutilized — compute resources. A new blog outlines the three main ways to achieve dynamic capacity management in Google Cloud: 1) scheduling capacity for planned downtime; 2) maintaining automated fallback capacity for unplanned downtime; and 3) relying on GKE’s core orchestration capabilities to automate resource allocation. 

Customer and partner updates

  • Business orchestration software provider UiPath was dealing with spiky workloads, and wanted more predictable costs. To get there, it re-architected its infrastructure, moving from isolated clusters to a shared Google Cloud GPU fleet that included both A3 VM instances (NVIDIA H100 GPUs) for training with G4 VM instances (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs) for inference. You can read more about their architecture here. 

  • Mirendil, an frontier AI lab focused on accelerating AI development, announced that it is using AI Hypercomputer with both TPUs and NVIDIA GPUs to support its model pre-training and post-training applications. 

  • Replenit, a retail CRM provider, built its AI decision engine in Google Cloud, using BigQuery, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and open-source Gemma models that it runs on Cloud TPUs. This latter combination provided Replenit with 90% lower pipeline costs than their previous cloud provider, the company reports. Read the full case study for more. 

  • Malachyte architected its AI-powered e-commerce recommendation platform on top of Bigtable, Managed Service for Apache Kafka, Pub/Sub, Compute Engine, and last but not least, GKE. See how it all comes together in this blog.

July 2026

Product, technology, and tools updates

  • Product update: Google Cloud Managed Lustre is now GA, and available in four distinct performance tiers that deliver throughput ranging from 125 MB/s, 250 MB/s, 500 MB/s, to 1000 MB/s per TiB of capacity — with the ability to scale up to 8 PB of storage capacity. The Managed Lustre solution is powered by DDN’s EXAScaler, combining DDN's decades of leadership in high-performance storage with Google Cloud's expertise in cloud infrastructure.

  • Product update: C4N network and storage optimized VMs are now GA. C4N is our first network- and block-storage-optimized VM series built to eliminate data-transfer bottlenecks. Powered by 5th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable processors and built on Google's Titanium offloading hardware, it achieves 400 Gbps network bandwidth, 95 million packets per second (MPPS), and up to 25 GiB/s of block storage throughput when paired with Hyperdisk Extreme.

  • New feature: GKE Dataplane V2 up to 15K Nodes with Network Policies (GA). This capability enables standard GKE clusters to scale up to 15,000 nodes while maintaining full active Network Policy enforcement, supporting the massive infrastructure needs of large enterprise and AI/ML customers.

  • New feature: Co-operative time-slicing in llm-d. If you’re running reinforcement learning (RL) workloads, you can now interleave independent RL jobs onto shared physical hardware, increasing aggregate accelerator duty cycles from a ~40% baseline up to 70% without impacting model convergence or accuracy. 

  • New AI security tool: Looking to secure your AI supply chain on GKE, deploy AI workloads safely, and cut down on shadow AI? We open-sourced k8s-aibom, a lightweight, unprivileged Kubernetes controller that continuously monitors container clusters to automatically detect running AI runtimes (like vLLM and Triton) and generate standard CycloneDX Machine Learning Bill of Materials (ML-BOMs). Check out the k8s-aibom project and get involved.

Practitioner guides and how-tos

  • How-to guide: On July 27, Google announced Day 0 support for Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model, the day weights were released. Whichever your preferred deployment path — via Model Garden, custom orchestration, or GKE with llm-d recipes — this guide offers detailed step-by-step instructions to help you evaluate and pilot Kimi K3 in Google Cloud. 

  • How-to guide: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) managed DRANET supports both GPUs and TPUs. There are several configurations to use this implementation, including standard cluster (where you have full control) and autopilot cluster (where Google does the heavy configs for you). Take a deeper dive in the hands-on lab, GKE Autopilot clusters with TPUs, GKE managed DRANET and Gemma 4.

  • How-to guide: Learn to run Ray on TPUs, not GPUs. In Part 1 of this two-part series, we discuss TPU slices (hint: Ray thinks of them as just another accelerator on which to schedule), then walk through Ray’s various AI libraries (Part 2).

  • How-to guide: Evaluate TPUs for sample workloads using a new microbenchmark suite that helps you accurately assess whether a device is achieving its theoretical performance specifications, and to identify specific performance gaps or architecture-specific bottlenecks. Dive in here. 

  • How-to guide: Scale your agents without killing your budget. Learn how GKE orchestration can help you safely pack more agents onto a fixed compute footprint with GKE Agent Sandbox and Pod snapshots. Whether your goal is performance or cost optimization, we teach you how to turn the right dials for optimal agent efficiency. 

  • Technical blueprint: Inside the optimization of Mistral 3 large inference on Ironwood. This blog outlines how one Google team optimized Mistral 3 large MoE model inference on Google’s Ironwood (TPU v7x), achieving a 1.5x performance gain. They did so with hybrid sharding, replacing linear VPU summations with tree reductions, optimizing GMM/MLA kernels, and adopting asynchronous scheduling. As a result, they boosted throughput by up to 48% while maintaining benchmark accuracy neutrality. Read the full blog here.

Research, reports and deep-dives

  • Report: Google was named a Leader in the inaugural GartnerⓇ Magic Quadrant™ for AI Infrastructure, positioned highest for ‘Ability to Execute’ and furthest for ‘Completeness of Vision’. Gartner called out Google’s proprietary scalable compute, integrated AI Hypercomputer architecture, and the scale of our AI compute capacity as key strengths. Download a copy here.

  • Report: We recently surveyed more than 1,400 senior IT leaders for our State of AI Infrastructure report, and a resounding pattern emerged: The gap between AI ambition and infrastructure reality is widening. In fact, 83% of organizations say they require infrastructure upgrades to support production-grade agentic AI. Read the accompanying blog to understand how adapting your infrastructure to meet the demands that agentic applications place on your systems will help you move from pilot to production.

June 2026

Product, technology and tool updates

  • Product update: Protecting sensitive data used with AI is a critical part of advanced and secure cloud infrastructure. Confidential Computing cryptographically protects data in use in hardware-based Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) with verifiable data integrity, and is now available on the accelerator-optimized G4 machine series, featuring NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. Get started with Confidential G4 VMs and Confidential G4 GKE Nodes.

  • Developer resource: The new TPU Developer Hub is the place to go for model builders, optimizers, and developers to learn to unlock the full performance of Google Cloud TPUs. Read more in this blog. 

  • New product: Scale your AI workloads with the new OpenTelemetry-Based TPU AI Telemetry Collector Agent. For the first time, you can route high-fidelity TPU hardware telemetry to Google Cloud Monitoring, Google Managed Prometheus, or your own self-hosted Grafana stack.

Practitioner guides and how-tos

  • How-to guide: Learn how to build high availability into an AI inference workload running on GKE Inference Gateway with TPUs, Cloud Storage FUSE and Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). This blog provides an overview, or you can get all the technical details in the hands-on codelab.

  • How-to guide: Did you know you can connect your AI agents to unstructured data in Cloud Storage via Model Context Protocol (MCP)? In this blog, learn about why would want to do that from three customer examples, then how to do it, choosing either a fully managed service, or a self-managed local server for more customization and control. 

Research, reports and deep-dives

  • Report: According to an independent benchmark report, GKE Inference Gateway outperforms the next leading managed Kubernetes service with 15.7% higher throughput, 92.8% shorter wait times, and 62.6% lower inter-token latency. This performance can be attributed to its use of prefix caching, which optimizes LLM performance by storing the KV cache (activation states) of long, repetitive prompt prefixes. Learn more in the blog. 

  • Architecture deep dive: A closer look at the cold start problem, this time for TPUs and GKE, and how the Run:ai Model Streamer can help change the dynamic. 

Customer and partner updates

  • Customer win: Leveraging GKE, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Pager Health is eliminating operational fragmentation to deliver a simplified, personalized U.S. healthcare experience that transforms lives.

  • Customer win: Trustpilot, the customer review platform, built a high-volume streaming pipeline using fine-tuned Gemma models with Dataflow and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform running on cost-optimized A2 VMs using A100 GPUs, as well as optimized version of vLLM maintained by Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

May 2026

Product, technology and tool updates

  • Product update: GKE Agent Sandbox is now generally available.

  • New open-source project: Agent Substrate is a new open-source project aimed at continuing to push the limits of agentic infrastructure density

  • New feature: Google AI Edge Portal, a solution for testing and benchmarking on-device machine learning (ML) at scale, now supports benchmarking and debugging on-device LLMs. Read more here. 

  • Product deep dive: We went into depth about Cloud Storage Rapid, a new family of high-performance storage offerings for AI workloads. At launch, offerings include Rapid Bucket (formerly Rapid Storage), a high-performance zonal object storage offering, and Rapid Cache (formerly Anywhere Cache), which accelerates reads on-demand and colocates compute and data for workloads in existing buckets. 

Research, reports and deep dives

  • Architecture deep dive: Google Global Infrastructure VP Bikash Koley and Engineering Fellow Arjun Singh provide a high-level overview of the challenges that AI workloads pose to network infrastructure, and discuss the deep enhancements we’ve made to our data center fabrics, WAN, and global networks to better support them. 

  • Architecture deep dive: We unveiled a new cluster-level reliability model for developing frontier AI models on TPUs, ditching instance-level reliability 

Customer and partner updates

  • Customer win: Visual media provider Imgix serves more than 8 billion images and videos from AI Hypercomputer equipped with G4 VMs powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.

items.title: Show HN: Spinf-serve – inference server for bulk scoring and decisions
items.story_key: story|title:spinf serve inference server for bulk scoring and decisions
items.content_excerpt: Bulk classification and decision inference on one GPU: the content is read once, every question about it is scored in the same pass. OpenAI-compatible, Apache 2.0 spinf-serve reads a piece of content once and answers many questions about it in the same pass. Each answer is a probability over the options you give, not generated text. It runs on one 24 GB NVIDIA GPU and serves an OpenAI-compatible API, the same API as the hosted spinf service. Apache 2.0. We built this engine for our own work: a daily market index read from millions of news articles, each article asked dozens of narrow, calibrated questions. A serving engine built for chat re-reads the content for every question and generates one token at a time, which made that job slow and expensive. spinf-serve lays every question out as a branch of one read of the content and packs many contents into one forward pass. Bulk classification is where it started and where it is strongest. The same mechanism is what is now called a decision model : a model that returns a probability over a fixed set of answers (yes or no, a label, a level) instead of a paragraph. Any open instruction model works this way in spinf-serve, and dedicated decision models run as they are. The hosted spinf API grew out of this engine; we are publishing it because people asked to run it on their own hardware. It is not a chat server. Nothing is generated unless you ask for it, and it is built for throughput rather than for the latency of a single request. Linux, an NVIDIA GPU with 24 GB and fp8 tensor cores (Ada, Hopper or Blackwell: RTX 4090 / 5090, L4, L40S, RTX 6000 Ada, H100), a driver supporting CUDA 13, Python 3.12. Ampere cards run with int8 weights instead ( configuration ). Or the image, with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed (the volume keeps the model and the compile caches; arguments after the image name are those of spinf-serve serve ): Then ask. Two classifications and one extraction from a single read of the content: For each scored question the response gives every option's probability, and the same probability on empty content (real numbers from the 12B model): p is the probability among your options. floor_p is the same question with no content, so p - floor_p is what the content added (here topic moves " billing" from 0.47 to 0.91). residual is the probability that went to words outside your options. For month the response lists the most likely answers with their probabilities ("September" first). The same body

items.content_excerpt: Today we’re announcing the biggest improvement to our provider routing algorithm since the founding of OpenRouter. Until now, our default router mostly rewarded providers for one thing: a low price. The new router rewards the inference that is actually best for you: cheap, but also fast, high-throughput, and reliable. Providers that deliver more value automatically win more traffic, so every provider has a reason to keep improving. That means the inference you get through OpenRouter keeps getting faster, more reliable, and more cost-effective, and you don’t have to change a line of code. It’s already working. The new algorithm has unlocked significant improvements in TTFT (16.9%), throughput (16.3%) and capacity errors (a remarkable 46% reduction!), with only minor increases in cost (6.0%). That’s before providers have had any time to optimize for the new algorithm. See our full experimental results for more details. Routing is still cache-aware, so once we’ve sent you to a provider, your session stays put as long as the cache is warm. Want price-only routing? You can still have it. See pinning and sorting providers in What stays the same . Most traffic (~77% of requests) on OpenRouter goes to models served by more than one provider. When a request doesn’t include an explicit sort or provider list, we need to pick a provider to send it to. Until now, we made that choice based almost entirely on input token price. The less expensive a provider was, the greater percentage of traffic it would receive, and any failed request was re-routed to the next cheapest option. This price-only approach got users the lowest prices in the ecosystem, but it created some unintended consequences: We wanted to ensure a marketplace where competing providers won traffic by serving better inference, not just cheaper inference. The new routing algorithm constantly monitors the performance of each provider to calculate a real-time Routing Cost that captures what a user pays for a good answer. The Routing Cost encompasses the price in actual dollars and cents, the cost of time spent waiting for a response, and the cost of retries when a provider fails or provides an unusable response. For each request, the router estimates how many input and output tokens it will use from the model’s recent traffic. items.title: Show HN: Omneum – Local, text-blind context control plane for AI agents
items.story_key: story|title:omneum local text blind context control plane for ai agents
items.content_excerpt: Text-blind context control plane for AI agents. Select high-utility context under token budgets. Omneum is an open-source context control plane for AI agents, built to optimize the evidence entering an LLM's context window. Agents accumulate context from retrieval, tools, memory, and previous sessions, but longer context windows don't guarantee better reasoning. Context rot can slowly degrade downstream answer accuracy even when the relevant information has already been retrieved. Provenance-aware graph inference: Iteratively computes source reliability and claim support across a bipartite graph, accounting for shared evidence origins and dependencies between sources. Context reconstruction: Selects original retrieved passages based on question relevance and incremental claim coverage within a token budget. Text-blind evaluation: Evaluates structured observations without reading source text strings or invoking an LLM judge. Local by default: Persists your agents' observations across sessions in a Context Graph , backed by SQLite or PostgreSQL. Compare retrieval-order packing with Omneum's claim-coverage selection under the same context budget. Packing chunks in retrieval order consumes 75 units while covering only two claims. Omneum retains two original chunks covering all four, using 32% less context capacity . Omneum uses a graph-based mathematical analysis, calculated from Observation objects, to estimate the structural reliability of sources and the support for claims found in retrieved context. Importantly, this analysis does not naively assume every source has derived its information independently. The same information often propagates across multiple sources. Without dependency tracking, five observations from different sources can be difficult to distinguish from five reports derived from the same upstream source. How much support should that claim receive? That depends partly on the reliability of the sources reporting it. But how do we determine the reliability of the sources? By looking at the claims they support. This definition seems circular, and it is. Nonetheless, it provides a well-defined notion of reliability that helps distinguish strongly supported context from weakly supported context. Of course claim-level scores are only useful for context selection if they can be mapped back to chunks. To bridge this gap, Omneum stores a claim-to-chunk mapping: each chunk retains its original text and chunk_id , while its associated claim_ids refer

items.title: DoorDash Cuts Grocery Reorder Latency from 16 to 2 Seconds with AI Agents
items.summary:
DoorDash reduced grocery reorder latency from 16 to 2 seconds by precomputing recurring purchase needs using batch LLM inference and deterministic validation. Live catalog resolution keeps product selections current, while an editable shopping interface avoids unnecessary model calls. The company reports that shopping list views doubled and the flow’s order rate increased by approximately 34%

By Leela Kumili

items.title: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
items.summary: When one AI agent tells another that "the tests passed" or "a person approved this refund", the receiver has only the sender's word. A2A and MCP authenticate the channel, but the sender is the party in doubt, so a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. We present Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol in which each claim carries evidence: records from an append-only Merkle log that the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs, signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control. Receivers check messages offline and give each claim a three-valued result: proven, unproven or failed. A claim that rests only on the agent's own report is never proven. Authority travels as grant chains rooted in a recorded human approval, and the chains can only narrow. We specify four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules that survive restarts, and strict readings that make independent verifiers agree, and we prove the resulting security properties. On a pre-specified benchmark of 926 messages from real runs, 712 of them lies in 16 classes, PCM accepts 10 lies, all of them stale evidence (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%). Plain A2A accepts all 712, and models of six deployed protocols (A2A with signed Agent Cards, uAgents, RFC 9421, SCITT, AP2, Verifiable Intent) accept 504-712. Two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts, and verification takes about 1 ms.

items.title: When to Assist and What to Suggest: Joint Gating and Memory-Grounded Hint Generation in One Compact Decoder
items.summary: Proactive assistants offer short, memory-grounded hints during a conversation, deciding when to assist and what to suggest. Current systems split this between a gate and a larger generator; we evaluate both together on 28,058 decision points. Stage-wise generation scores are oracle-gate ceilings: behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against a ceiling of 0.2971, and end-to-end precision is 0.2387, leaving substantial headroom. A gate pays off through precision and compute, whose saving falls from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one. The memory profile drives hint quality: removing it costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match. One 1B decoder can do both, gating from an intermediate layer and generating in the same pass. At its final checkpoint it matches or exceeds the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline; across three seeds, its deeper exit ties the separate gate. A human evaluation (1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues) supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one. Graded metrics and LlamaPIE's native judge track human ratings more closely than exact match, which we report as a strict lower bound.

items.title: Preserving Utility in Continual LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Projections
items.summary: Unlearning concerns the task of removing the influence of a sensitive portion of the training data, such as protected, copyrighted or private text, from a model without retraining it from scratch. While unlearning requests happen continuously during a model's lifetime, the vast majority of LLM unlearning methods are ill-suited for iterated removal, yielding steep decay in forgetting and utility upon sequential unlearning. This decay stems from interference between successive updates, as each new deletion can undo earlier ones or push the model further along directions already degraded by them. To address this, we introduce Continual Orthogonal Projection (COP), a gradient-projection scheme that restricts each update to the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from prior forget sets. This approach provably guarantees first-order non-interference with earlier deletions. COP stores only a low-rank basis per layer, requiring neither past gradients nor previous forget sets, and plugs into unlearning methods that update the model through gradient steps on a differentiable loss without modifying its objective. Experiments on standard LLM unlearning benchmarks (TOFU and RWKU) show that COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting, preventing the collapse of standard objectives and forgetting more effectively than continual-specific baselines.

items.title: Retrieving from Your Own Mistakes: On-Policy Training of Embedding Models for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: Complex questions in retrieval-augmented generation require evidence spread over several documents, and an answer is reliable only when the retriever finds all of it. Chain embedding retrievers collect such evidence step by step, re-encoding the question together with the passages retrieved so far, and we find that they are already strong: trained only on gold histories, a small chain embedding retriever that calls no language model outperforms graph-based systems and is competitive with a search agent. This training, however, leaves a gap. At test time the retriever conditions on its own retrievals, which soon contain mistakes: by the third step, about half or more of the states it visits hold a wrong passage, and these passages lower its chance of retrieving a missing gold passage well beyond what the difficulty of the states explains. We propose on-policy state training, which trains the encoder on the states it reaches itself. At every epoch the current encoder retrieves chains for the training questions; each state it visits, including those built on its own mistakes, is labeled with the earliest gold passage still missing while the other missing gold passages are masked, so that no correct continuation is penalized; and the encoder is updated contrastively on these states mixed with teacher-forced ones, so that its training distribution follows it as it learns. The resulting retriever retrieves complete evidence more often than teacher-forced training and the systems we compare, and it transfers without further training to harder long-chain variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA that we construct. On the same states, it recovers from its own mistakes far more often, and controlled comparisons attribute the gain to training on the states the encoder currently reaches.

items.story_key: story|title:things that go beep in the night agentic ai joins the search for extraterrestria
items.content_excerpt: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.” Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold. At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI , a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther , a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS . Nexus , a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. items.title: claude-code v2.1.310
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added the Monitor tool and plugin monitors on Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry, and when telemetry or nonessential traffic is disabled; long foreground sleeps are now blocked there too
  • Fixed requests failing behind some gateways and compatible servers that reject the effort-2025-11-24 beta value or mid-conversation system messages; Claude Code now retries without them
  • Fixed background cleanup deleting some recent files, such as pasted images, when cleanupPeriodDays is set to a very large value
  • Fixed compaction after a "Prompt is too long" error keeping too much of a conversation with dense text, such as base64 or SVG, so the next request could fail again
  • Fixed file read permission prompts not showing where a symbolic link leads
  • Fixed a question's auto-continue timeout firing the moment the external editor closed after a long edit
  • Windows: Fixed PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks letting a tool call through when Git Bash is missing and the hook's command is only quoted strings, such as a quoted path
  • Improved auto mode's prompt before the first read outside the working directories: it now says when blocking those reads makes shell commands ask for permission
  • Improved memory use of non-interactive sessions (-p, Agent SDK) during compaction when the transcript file is very large
  • Improved a mod's Image to draw inside tmux with allow-passthrough and focus-events on, in kitty, Ghostty, and iTerm2 3.5+ with fullscreen rendering, where it showed only its alt text
  • Linux: Improved /sandbox and the sandbox startup warning to name Ubuntu's AppArmor restriction on user namespaces, and how to lift it, when it keeps bubblewrap from starting the sandbox
  • Changed the error for an MCP tool call that times out in a non-interactive session while the server's elicitation is unanswered: it now tells Claude that no answer came and not to repeat the call
  • [VSCode] Fixed pressing Enter on the plan review card's "Send feedback and keep planning" button approving the plan instead of sending your comments back
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing "Something went wrong" after "Switch branch & continue" on a cloud session opened from Session history's Web tab
  • [Cloud sessions] Added Claude Code cloud sessions and Remote Control permissions to Enterprise custom roles, so Owners can control access to each by role
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Choose file button to load a cloud environment's setup script from a file
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed saves and archives in the cloud environment edit dialog showing no error inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed routine API token actions showing only a toast; the error now appears in the routine edit dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the session start checklist to show a cloud environment's setup script output in a scrolling box
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed turning on Cloud sessions or Remote Control in admin settings to ask for confirmation and list the custom roles that have that permission
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the cloud environment dialog to open network access, setup script and environment variables from rows instead of listing every editor at once
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag treating ! commands such as !restart and !help as ordinary messages when sent in bold, italic or strikethrough
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag admin channel and workspace pages being replaced by a load error when a background refresh of the bundle list fails
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag's spend limits page in admin settings reporting that no channels match a filter while channel names are still loading
  • [Code Review] Fixed the Code Review admin section hiding its repositories and switches after a failed refresh of the repository list
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review admin section to retry the first load and show one Try again banner when it still fails
